title: Game 2: Hans vs Magnus
notes: Game 2 of 12 in the experiment, from the Ruy Lopez. Magnus (the learner) reads his notebook and similar past mistakes before every move; Hans (the control) has neither.

Nf6 hits my e4 pawn, but 5.O-O Nxe4 6.Re1 Nf6 7.Nxe5 Nxe5 8.Rxe5+ regains the pawn with an active rook and a big development lead, while 5.Nxe5 Nxe5 6.d4 fails to Nxe4. Castling develops safely and keeps the e-file resource, so I'll take the king to safety.

White's bishop on a4 is loose, so ...b5 gains a tempo and forces it to b3 before I complete development; I checked 6.Bxc6 dxc6 and 6.Nxe5 Nxe5 7.d4 bxa4, both of which leave me at least fine or a piece up. I also verified no enemy pawn push punishes b5 immediately — a4 later just invites ...Rb8 or ...b4.

Black's b5 hits my bishop, and Bxb5 axb5 loses a piece since I have no knight on c3 to recapture, so retreating is required. Bb3 keeps the bishop on the strong a2-g8 diagonal eyeing f7 and prepares c3/d4 or Re1, which is the standard Ruy Lopez setup; Nxe4 would just be met by Re1 or d4 regaining the pawn with initiative.

This is exactly the Open Spanish move order — 6...Nxe4 transposes to the main line after 7.d4 d5 8.dxe5 Be6, where I grab a central pawn and get active play. I checked the sharp replies: 7.Bd5 Nf6 8.Bxc6 dxc6 is fine for me, and 7.Nxe5 Nxe5 8.Re1 holds nothing since I can defend with d5/Be7, so the knight capture is sound.

Black has grabbed the e4 pawn, so I want to open the centre immediately with d4, striking at e5 and preparing Re1 to hit the loose knight on e4. After 7.d4 exd4 8.Re1 d5 9.Nxd4 I regain material with strong central pressure, and 7...Nxd4 8.Nxd4 exd4 9.Re1 also wins the knight back.

This is the Open Variation of the Spanish by transposition, and ...d5 is the main line: it gives my e4 knight a solid pawn support while blocking the b3 bishop's diagonal. After 8.dxe5 Be6 I get the standard setup with ...Be7/...O-O, and I avoid loose-piece problems since the knight is no longer hanging to Nxe5/Re1 tricks.

This is the Open Variation of the Ruy Lopez, and the main line here is to grab the e5 pawn with the pawn, keeping a strong e5 wedge and preparing c3/Nbd2 to challenge the knight on e4. If Black tries 8...Nxe5 9.Nxe5 Nxe5 (or Qd6), I stay comfortable with Re1 and Bxd5 ideas, so I'll follow theory.

This is the Open Spanish main line after 8.dxe5, and the standard developing move is ...Be6, which solidly backs up the d5 pawn and supports my strong knight on e4 while no enemy pawn can ever harass the bishop there (d5 is mine, f-pawn is on f2). I checked alternatives like ...Nxe5 (loses the e4 knight to Re1 ideas and Nxe5) and ...Bb7 (leaves d5 under-defended after c4 ideas), so Be6 is best.

This is the Open Variation of the Spanish, and after 8...Be6 the main line is to shore up the center with c3, supporting d4 ideas and keeping the b3 bishop's diagonal while preparing Nbd2 to challenge the e4 knight. Grabbing with Bxd5 fails since after 9...Bxd5 10.Qxd5 Qxd5 I simply lose a piece, and Nd4 just helps Black trade off pieces.

This is the main line Open Spanish, where 9...Bc5 is the standard developing move: it puts the bishop on an active diagonal where no pawn can hit it, adds pressure to f2 to support my knight on e4, and prepares castling. I checked White's replies (Nbd2, Qd3, Bc2) and none win a piece, whereas passive moves like Be7 let White gain time with Qd3/Nbd2.

This is the Open Variation of the Ruy Lopez with 9...Bc5, where the main line is to challenge the strong e4 knight with my own knight development. I considered Qe2 and Nbd2; Nbd2 is best since it attacks the e4 knight and prepares Bc2, and the Dilworth sacrifice 10...Nxf2 11.Rxf2 Bxf2+ 12.Kxf2 f6 13.exf6 Qxf6 leaves me with enough material (rook and knight for bishop and two pawns).

This is the main line Open Spanish; castling is the standard developing move, getting my king safe and connecting rooks while the knight on e4 is still well supported by d5 and Be6. Bxf2+ would only win two pawns for a bishop after Rxf2 Nxf2 Kxf2, which my notebook warns against, and Nxd2 just trades off my best-placed piece.

This is the main line of the Open Ruy Lopez, and 11.Bc2 is the standard move: it saves the bishop from the b3-pawn-chain pressure, adds a second attacker on the e4-knight, and keeps the dangerous Bc2/Qd3 battery ideas alive. The immediate 11.Bxd5 Bxd5 12.Nxe4 Bxe4 just trades off my attackers for nothing, and 11...Nxf2 12.Rxf2 Bxf2+ 13.Kxf2 only gives Black rook and pawn for two pieces.

This is the Open Spanish main line after 11.Bc2, and ...f5 is the principled move: it cements my strong knight on e4 so it can't be chased away, and it keeps my pieces mutually supported instead of leaving the e4 knight loose to Nxe4 or Nb3/Ng5 harassment. I considered the sharp Dilworth 11...Nxf2 12.Rxf2 Bxf2+ 13.Kxf2 but that gives two pieces for a rook and pawn, which my rules warn against, so I prefer the solid main line.

This is the Open Spanish; the main theoretical continuation here is 12.Nb3, hitting the c5-bishop and preparing Nfd4 to challenge the strong knight on e4 and Black's center. I checked 12...Nxf2 13.Rxf2 Bxf2+ 14.Kxf2, where White emerges a piece up for two pawns with the king safe enough after Kg1 ideas.

My bishop on c5 is attacked by the knight that just came to b3, so I must move it; Bb6 keeps it on the strong a7-g1 diagonal, out of reach of any pawn push, and still eyes f2/g1. I rejected Bxf2+ because Rxf2 Nxf2 Kxf2 gives only two pawns for a piece, and my e4 knight stays safely propped up by the d5 pawn against Bc2.

Black's knight on e4 is strong, so I want to challenge the center while keeping my f3-knight as a kingside defender — after 13.Nbd4 Nxd4 I can answer 14.cxd4, holding the e5/d4 chain with Nf3 still guarding my king (unlike 13.Nfd4, which invites the ...f4/...Ng3 attacking plans). Tactically 13...Nxe5 fails to 14.Nxe6 forking queen and rook, and 13...Bxd4 14.cxd4 just hands me the bishop pair and a big center.

White's Nd4 hits both my Nc6 and Be6, so I resolve the tension by taking the most active piece first: 13...Nxd4, and if 14.Nxd4 I follow with Bxd4 15.cxd4 c5 to hit the d4/e5 chain, while my Ne4 stays solidly supported by the d5 pawn. I checked the alternatives — Nxe5 loses material to Nxe6 forking queen and rook, and Nxc3/Nxf2 just drop a piece.

Recapturing with the pawn keeps my strong d4–e5 chain and the bishop pair, and crucially 14...Bxd4 now just loses a piece because after 15.Nxd4 the knight is defended by my queen along the d-file (15...Qxd4 16.Qxd4). I also keep my f3 knight as an extra defender of f2/h2 against Black's ...Qh4 and ...Nxf2 tricks, while Rc1 later can press c7.

White's natural plan is f3 kicking my strong e4 knight, so I grab space with f4, which both secures the knight (after f3 it jumps to g3 hitting the rook) and cramps White's kingside; Bxd4 just loses a piece to Nxd4, and c5 or retreats concede my best piece's post. After 15.Bxe4 dxe4 I keep the bishop pair and a useful e4/f4 pawn wedge.

Black's knight on e4 is only defended by the d5 pawn, so Qd3 adds a second attacker (threatening Bxe4 dxe4 Qxe4 to win a pawn) while also covering d4 so that the ...Nxf2 Rxf2 Bxd4 trick fails to Qxd4. If Black answers 15...Bf5 to defend the knight I'll step off the b1-h7 diagonal with Qd2, keeping pressure on the weak f4 pawn.

I first checked the tempting "defend f4" queen moves and saw that Qh4, Qg5, Qf6 and Qd6/Nd6/Nf6 all lose material (Nf3 covers g5/h4, the e5 pawn captures on d6/f6), and Bxd4 just drops a piece to Nxd4. So instead I attack the overworked Nf3 — the defender of d4, e5, g5 and h4 — with Bg4: if 16.Bxf4 Bxf3 17.Qxf3 Bxd4 regains the pawn, and 17.gxf3 Qg5+ or 16.h3 Bxf3 leave White's king and d4 pawn loose, while Bh5 is a safe retreat square.

Black's Bg4 adds pressure to f3, but his f4 pawn is simply loose, and taking it with the dark-squared bishop keeps d4 covered by my queen while killing the ...f3 break. The tactical try 16...Nxf2 17.Rxf2 Bxf2+ 18.Kxf2 Bxf3 19.Qxf3 leaves me a point up with two bishops, and 17...Rxf4 18.Rxf4 Bxf3 19.Rxf3 just loses material for Black.

White's bishop that just captured on f4 is completely undefended — Rf1 is blocked by its own f2/f3, and neither Qd3 nor Bc2 nor Nf3 covers f4 — while the f-file from f8 is wide open. My knight on e4 is attacked twice but held by the d5 pawn, so after Rxf4 the obvious Bxe4 dxe4 Qxe4 line leaves me a bishop up for a pawn (and ...Bxf3 follows), so I simply take the free piece instead of grabbing pawns with Nxf2 or Bxd4.

I'm down a bishop for a pawn after the exchange on f4, so I need activity, and I noticed that Black's rook on f4 is completely undefended — Qe3 hits it diagonally while also eyeing e4 and shoring up d4 and f2. Tactical checks: 17...Rxf3 18.gxf3! forks the bishop and knight with the pawn, 17...Nxf2 18.Qxf4 just wins the rook, and 17...Bxf3 18.Qxf4 Bxg2 19.Kxg2 leaves me ahead, so Black must retreat and I gain a tempo.

My rook on f4 is attacked by Qe3, and I'm a clean bishop-for-pawn up, so I just need the safest consolidating retreat — Rf7 is defended by my king, keeps the rook flexible, and leaves nothing loose (Ne4 is held by d5, and White's f-pawn can never kick it while his own knight sits on f3). I rejected the more active Rf5 because it stays undefended and 18.Nh4 would hit it with tempo, and Bxd4 loses material to 18.Qxd4 hitting both rook and knight.

I'm down a bishop for a pawn, so I need active play: h3 hits the undefended bishop on g4 and sets up tactics on the e4 knight. If 18...Bxf3 19.Qxf3 the knight on e4 is attacked twice and only defended by the d5 pawn, and 18...Nxf2 19.Rxf2 Bxf3 20.gxf3 actually restores material equality for me.

I'm up a bishop for a pawn, and White's h3 forces my g4 bishop to decide; the cleanest consolidation is to trade off White's only active piece, the knight on f3, which also wrecks his kingside structure. Qxf3 loses to ...Nxf2! (Rxf2 Rxf3 wins the queen), so gxf3 is forced, after which my knight just steps back to d6 or g5 and I remain a knight up for a pawn against a shattered king position; Bf5 would instead invite g4 with tempo.

I'm already down material, so recapturing the bishop is essential; gxf3 would shatter my king's shield with Black's queen and rooks ready to use the open g-file. Qxf3 takes the bishop while keeping my pawn cover intact and adds a second attacker (with Bc2) on the knight on e4, which is only defended once by the d5 pawn.

My knight on e4 is attacked twice (Qf3, Bc2) and undefended, but the f-file is clear, so Rxf3! wins White's queen outright. After gxf3 the knight simply steps away (Nd6/Nf6/Nd2), leaving me queen-for-rook up on top of my extra piece.

Black's rook on f3 just took my queen, so I must recapture immediately with gxf3; every alternative (like Bxe4) loses far more material since the rook escapes with Rxf1+. After gxf3 Nxf2 I simply take Rxf2, and even though Bxd4 follows, my two rooks give reasonable play against the queen.

My knight on e4 is hit by both fxe4 and Bxe4, so it must move; with a queen-for-rook material edge I want a safe square that also keeps pressure. Nd2 is untouched by any pawn or piece, attacks Rf1 and the loose f3 pawn, and if White chases it with Rd1/Rf2 I have Nxf3+ forking back (Kg2 Nxd4 even hits the bishop), whereas Nxf2 would needlessly trade two pieces for a rook and pawns.

Black's knight on d2 forks my f1-rook and the f3-pawn, so I must move the rook and ideally with tempo. Rfd1 steps away while attacking the knight on d2 and reinforcing d4, whereas Rfe1 just lets Nxf3+ followed by Nxe1 picking up the rook for free. After Rfd1 Nxf3+ Kg2 Nxd4 I can answer Bb3 to trade off the annoying knight.

I noticed my knight on d2 is actually hanging — my queen's path to d2 is blocked by my own d5 pawn, so Rd1 threatens to win it, meaning Bxd4 would lose the piece to Rxd2. Nxf3+ saves the knight with tempo, snatches a pawn, and after Kg2 the knight can continue with Nxd4 (protected by my Bb6, so Rxd4 Bxd4 just loses a rook) or retreat safely to g5, keeping my decisive material edge.

The knight on f3 is undefended, so Kg2 attacks it and forces it to retreat (Ne1+ or Nd2 drop to Rxe1/Rxd2, and Nxe5/Nxd4 lose it for a pawn). If Black tries 22...Qg5+ I simply take with 23.Kxf3, winning the piece, since f3 isn't covered by the queen and h3 guards g4 against Qg4+.

My knight on f3 is attacked by the king, so I must move it, and Nxd4 is the best square: it grabs a central pawn, is defended by my Bb6, and attacks the Bc2, so if Rxd4 Bxd4 I trade a knight for a rook and pawn while already up a queen for a rook. Nxe5 also wins a pawn but is less forcing and leaves White's d4 pawn and bishop active.

My bishop on c2 is attacked by the knight, and Rxd4 just loses a rook for the knight since Bb6 recaptures. I'm already down material (Q+N vs R+B), so I want to eliminate Black's annoying centralized knight: Bb3 saves the bishop, adds pressure to d5, and invites Nxb3 axb3, which opens the a-file against a6 and trades off Black's most active attacker.

I'm up a queen and knight for a rook plus a pawn, so the simplest path is to trade off White's only active piece: Nxb3 removes the bishop that was pressuring my d5 pawn, and after axb3 my a6 pawn is still guarded by Ra8 and d5 by my queen. That leaves Q+R+B against two rooks with no counterplay, which is trivially winning.

I'm down heavy material, so I must at least recover the bishop — axb3 regains the piece and keeps my pawn structure somewhat intact. Rxd5 instead loses a rook to Qxd5+, and leaving the knight on b3 is just giving away a piece for nothing.

Bxf2 is poisoned since Kxf2 just wins the bishop, so instead I use my big material edge (Q+R+B vs two rooks) to grab White's loose e5 pawn with tempo: Qg5+ forces the king to move or a rook to block, and after Qxe5 my queen is centralized and also guards d5 against Rxd5 (Qxd5+ would win the rook).

I must move out of check, and Kh2 would allow Qxe5+ picking up my e-pawn with tempo, while Kh1 leaves f2 hanging to both the queen and the b6 bishop. Kf1 keeps f2 defended by the king, avoids any immediate follow-up check except Qc4+ (which I answer with Kg2 or Ke1), and keeps my king connected to the rooks so I can follow with Re1 to fight for the e-file.

I'm up a bishop and a rook's worth of material (Q+R+B vs two rooks), so I just consolidate and grab the loose e5 pawn: Qxe5 centralizes my queen while defending d5 and b5 along the rank, so White's rooks have no entry (Rxd5 loses a rook, Ra5 is harmless since a6 is covered by my rook). Bxf2 would be a blunder since Kxf2 just wins my bishop.

I'm down material (two rooks vs queen and bishop), and captures fail — Rxd5 drops a rook to Qxd5, and Rxa6 drops it to Rxa6 since the a8 rook covers that square. Rd2 is the solid choice: it guards both b2 (stopping Qxb2) and f2, keeping my second-rank pawns and blocking the e5–a1 diagonal.

I spotted that Qxb2 loses my queen to Rxd2-b2 since the rook guards b2 along the second rank, and Qe1+/Qe2+ also drop the queen to Rxe1/Rxe2 — so I checked every capture first. Instead Qc3 forks both undefended rooks on a1 and d2 while hitting b2, and if White defends with Rdd1 the b2 pawn falls anyway, keeping my queen-and-bishop-for-rook material edge.

review.label: blunder
review.refutation: 27. bxc3 c6 28. Re1 Kf7 29. Rde2 Bc5

moves.thought: Black's queen just landed on c3 where my b2 pawn can simply capture it — the pawn isn't pinned and the queen has no escape or counter-threat. After bxc3 I'm up a queen for nothing, with only a loose Bxf2 tactic that costs Black the bishop.

White's rook on d2 already attacks my loose d5 pawn, so I must address it first; 27...d4 fails to 28.cxd4 since Bxd4 is met by Rxd4 (the bishop would be undefended), and Rd8 alone invites Rad1 piling up on d5. Playing c6 gives d5 a pawn defender, keeps my whole 4-vs-2 queenside majority intact, and leaves Rd8/Kf7 to follow.

I'm up two rooks for a bishop, so I just need safe consolidation — Rxd5 and Rxa6 both lose a rook since c6 and the a8-rook defend those pawns. Doubling with Rad1 piles on the d5 pawn (only defended by c6), and if Black ever pushes d4 then cxd4 Bxd4 Rxd4 simply wins the bishop.

My d5 pawn is attacked twice by the rooks on the d-file and defended only by the c6 pawn, so Rxd5 cxd5 Rxd5 would just win a pawn and leave my bishop loose; pushes like d4, c5 or b4 all abandon d5 or drop material (d4 cxd4 Bxd4 Rxd4). Rd8 adds the second defender so any capture sequence on d5 simply loses material for White, and it activates my rook on the open file.

Black's d5 pawn is the only thing blocking my doubled rooks from the d-file, and the Bb6 is the lone recapturer on d8, so if the file opens, Rxd8+ Bxd8 Rxd8+ wins a piece. 29.c4 strikes at that pawn and at Black's queenside majority: 29...d4 30.cxd4 drops material to the doubled rooks, 29...dxc4 30.bxc4 bxc4 loses to Rxd8+, and quiet replies allow cxd5 with a dominating rook ending. Note Rxd5 fails immediately to cxd5.

White's c4 push hits my d5 pawn, so I resolve the tension favourably: 29...dxc4 forces 30.bxc4 bxc4, after which I have five pawns (a6, c6, c4, g7, h7) against White's two, with bishop plus three pawns balancing the extra rook — and any rook trade only improves my winning chances. I checked White's only captures (bxc4 and Rxd8+) plus 30.Rd7, and in each case ...cxb3/...c3 with Ba5 support keeps my queenside mass rolling.

review.label: blunder
review.refutation: 30. Rxd8+ Bxd8 31. Rxd8+ Kf7 32. bxc4 bxc4

moves.thought: I'm down a bishop and pawns, so my practical hope is to eliminate Black's dangerous queenside pawn mass and keep both rooks active rather than trade into a lost rook-versus-bishop ending. Taking with bxc4 removes the protected passer and leaves me doubled rooks pressuring the c4 pawn and the d-file, where Rd4 ideas give some counterplay.

My rook on d8 is attacked by the doubled rooks and defended only once by Bb6, so 31.Rxd8+ Bxd8 32.Rxd8+ would win the exchange — every other move (bxc4, b4, Bxf2, Rb8) allows exactly that. Trading immediately with Rxd2 is the cheapest way out: after 31.Rxd2 I keep bishop plus five pawns against rook plus three, and if White ever takes cxb5 axb5 I get connected b- and c-passers to push with king and bishop.

Black's rook on d2 is completely undefended — the bishop on b6 covers the c5-g1 diagonal, not d2 — so I simply win a full rook with the recapture. After Rxd2 bxc4 I'm a rook for a bishop ahead with an easily winning endgame.

Bxf2 just loses the bishop to Kxf2, and bxc4 leaves the c4 pawn on a light square my dark-squared bishop can never defend, so Rc2 would regain it. With c5 I freeze White's c4 pawn (it can never advance since Bb6 covers c5), keep b5 guarded by a6, and prepare connected queenside passers supported by bishop and king — a bishop plus two extra pawns should outrun the lone rook.

review.label: blunder
review.refutation: 32. Rd6 bxc4 33. Rxb6 h6 34. Rxa6 c3

moves.thought: My rook needs to be active against Black's queenside pawns rather than passive, and I must avoid trading rook for bishop+pawn since Black's connected passers plus bishop would win. Rd5 hits both b5 and c5 while keeping the c4/c5 tension; if Black pushes b4 I get Rb5 forking b4 and c5, and if Black ignores it, cxb5 axb5 Rxb5 wins a pawn.

My b5 pawn is hit twice (Rd5 and the c4 pawn) and only defended once, and after 32...b4 White's 33.Rb5 forks my loose bishop on b6 and the b4 pawn, so I'd end up just one pawn up. By taking with 32...bxc4 I liquidate White's only queenside pawn and keep a four-against-two pawn mass; if 33.Rd4 c3 I can meet 34.Rc4 with ...Bd4, defending both c5 and c3 (and Rxd4 cxd4 would leave me with winning passers).

The rook on d5 can swing to d6 where it forks the undefended bishop on b6 and the a6 pawn, so Black must move the bishop and I pick up a pawn with Rxa6. If instead 33...c3, then 34.Rxb6 c2 35.Rb1 stops the pawn and I'm a whole piece up.

My bishop on b6 is attacked by the rook, so I retreat it with tempo to c7, which attacks the rook on d6 and forces it to move while keeping my dark-squared bishop (the piece that controls c1 for the coming c-pawn promotion). Ba5 and Ba7 are worse because Rxa6 would hit the bishop again or leave it passive, and pushing c3 at once simply loses the bishop to Rxb6.

Black's doubled c-pawns on c5/c4 are loose, and Rc6 hits c5 while also lining up on the bishop; after 34...c3 35.Rxc5 both the bishop and the c3 pawn hang, and 34...Bd8 35.Rxc5 followed by Rxc4 nets two pawns. Compared to Rxa6, which only wins one pawn, this should restore material balance in my favour.

My c5 pawn and a6 pawn are both hit by the rook on c6, and only Bb6/Bd6 defends c5; I prefer Bd6 since after Rxa6 (which also hits the bishop on the 6th rank) the bishop has many safe retreats like Be5/Be7, whereas from b6 it is nearly trapped by the c5 pawn. Giving up a6 keeps four pawns (including the doubled c-pawns) plus bishop against rook and two pawns, which is better than ...a5 or ...c3 lines where I end up losing both c-pawns to Rxc5/Rxc3.

Black's bishop just moved to d6 where it is completely undefended — the c5 pawn cannot capture backwards and the king is far away on g8. Taking it leaves me a rook and two pawns against five scattered pawns, which is trivially winning.

I'm a rook down for pawns, so my only plan is to march the king toward my doubled passed c-pawns while keeping g7/h7 defended; pushing 35...c3 immediately just loses the pawn after 36.Rd1 c2 37.Rc1, and keeping the pawn on c5 usefully blocks the c-file in front of c4. I rejected Kf7 because 36.Rd7+ picks up g7 with check, whereas Kf8 keeps g7 guarded and lets my king head to e7/d6.

Black's only counterplay is the doubled c-pawns, and since they're on the same file a single rook holds them both, so I can safely grab the free a-pawn. After 36.Rxa6 c3 37.Ra3 the advanced pawn is attacked and indefensible, and the rook mops up on c3/c4, leaving me rook and two pawns up.

I'm a rook down for two pawns, so my only practical chance is the connected c-pawns; pushing c3 immediately just loses it to Rc6 or Ra1, so I need my king to come over and support the pawns. Ke7 heads for d6/d5 where the king defends c5 and escorts the c-pawns forward.

Black's doubled c-pawns are the only danger, so I want my rook on the c-file where it both attacks c5 and blocks the advance; after Rc6, Kd7 allows Rxc5 and Kd6 lets me drop back to c1 where the pawns are frozen while my king walks over. Any pawn push (c4-c3) just loses to Rxc3 or Rxc5 followed by mopping up.

My c5 pawn is hanging to the rook and cannot be defended, so the c-pawns are falling regardless; I want the move that fights hardest. Kd7 attacks the rook on c6 with tempo and brings my king toward the queenside pawns, whereas c3 just drops both pawns immediately after Rxc5.

I'm a full rook up with Black having only the c-pawns and kingside pawns, and Rxc5 snaps off a pawn while also attacking the c4 pawn. After Kd6 Rxc4 Kd5 I simply retreat the rook (e.g. Rg4) and remain rook-plus-pawns ahead, an easy win.

I'm down a rook for pawns, so my only practical chance is activity: Kd6 centralises the king and attacks the rook on c5, forcing it to move (Rxc4 keeps it hanging to my advancing king), whereas c3 just loses the pawn to Rxc3 immediately with no gain.

The black c4 pawn is undefended, and after Rxc4 I'm a rook up against just two kingside pawns, which my king and rook can easily contain while I push my own pawns. That's far simpler than cutting the king off with Rd5+.
I'm down a rook and can only play practically, so I want my king active; Kd5 directly attacks the rook on c4 and forces it to move, gaining a tempo while my king heads toward White's remaining pawns.

I'm up a full rook for two pawns, so the simplest path is to pick off Black's remaining pawns and promote my own. Rc7 attacks g7 and Black's king is too far away to defend it — after something like 40...Ke6 41. Rxg7 Kf6 42. Rxh7 I'm completely winning.

My rook on nothing — I'm a full rook down and White's rook on c7 already attacks g7, which I cannot defend (no king move reaches g7 and any pawn push just loses the other pawn to Rxh7). I'll keep the king as active as possible, heading toward White's f2/h3 pawns, rather than shuffling pawns that fall anyway.
Black's king on e6 can't defend the g7 pawn in time, and my rook on the seventh rank picks it up for free. After Rxg7 Kf6, Rxh7 nets both pawns leaving me a trivially winning rook-and-pawns endgame.

I'm down a rook for a pawn in a lost ending, so my only practical try is activity: Kf6 attacks the rook on g7, forcing it to move or capture h7, after which my king can harass it from g6 and I can at least keep the h-pawn question open. Pushing h5 or h6 just loses the pawn to Rg5/Rxh7 anyway while leaving my king passive.

I'm up a full rook with Black having only the h7 pawn left, so grabbing it leaves a trivially winning rook-and-three-pawns endgame against a bare king. The rook on h7 is safe since the black king on f6 can't reach it.

I'm down a rook and two pawns in a hopeless king-versus-rook-and-pawns ending, so my only practical try is to stay active and harass the rook. Kg6 attacks the rook on h7 and keeps my king centralized near White's pawns, forcing the rook to move.

My rook on h7 is attacked by the black king on g6, so I must move it to safety; Rg7+, Rh6+, Rh5 and Rf7 all lose the rook. Rh4 keeps the rook on the h-file guarding the pawn's advance and cuts the black king off from the fourth rank, after which I'll bring my king up and promote.

I'm just a bare king against rook and three pawns, so I play for maximum nuisance value; Kg5 attacks the rook on h4 and forces it to move while keeping my king active and centralized. Kf5 or Kg7 would be passive, and Kg5 is not covered by the rook or any pawn.

I'm up a rook and two pawns against a bare king, so I just need to advance safely and push the enemy king back. f4+ gains space with tempo, driving the king away from my pawns while my rook on h4 stays protected by the h3 pawn's neighbour structure and cannot be captured.

The rook on h4 is completely undefended — the h3 pawn only covers g4, so capturing it is free and removes White's last piece. After 44...Kxh4 45.f5 Kg5 I round up the f-pawn too, leaving a dead-drawn king-and-pawn ending instead of a hopeless one.

My h3 pawn is attacked by the black king, and pushing 45.f5 lets 45...Kg5 get in front of the pawn, after which I could end up with only the h-pawn and a drawn corner. So I play Kg2, defending h3 and keeping both pawns; then Kg3 shoulders the black king away and I advance the pawns with king support for a clean win.
Only one legal move exists — my king on h4 must go to h5, since h3 pawn and the g2 king cover everything else.

new_lessons: [middlegame] Before any queen or piece move, list every enemy PAWN that captures the destination square; a pawn defender refutes any fork or double attack Example: 26...Qc3 forked rooks on a1/d2 but 27.bxc3 simply took the queen for a pawn

[middlegame] When ahead, win material by force (hanging piece, clean pin) rather than by a fork; verify the forking square is attacked by nothing at all Example: At 98% winning, Qc3's "double attack" lost the queen; quiet Qe4 kept everything

[middlegame] Before every move, list your undefended pieces and squares where one enemy move hits two of them; fix the loosest first Example: Loose bishop plus loose pawn gave the opponent free tempo moves ...Nb4, ...d5, ...f5

[middlegame] Ask "what is my opponent's best pawn push/capture reply?" for each candidate; if a pawn gains tempo or wins material, pick another move Example: ...d5 and ...f5 chased a bishop with no retreat; bxc3 refuted Qc3

[endgame] With bishop plus pawns versus rook, keep pawns connected and defended by each other or the king; isolated pawns on open lines are eaten one by one Example: 29...dxc4 and 31...c5 left a6/c4/c6 scattered; Rd6-b6-a6 collected them all

[endgame] When choosing a recapture with the enemy rook active, pick the one that keeps your pawn chain linked, even if it concedes a doubled pawn Example: 29...bxc4 kept c6+c4+a6 linked; 29...dxc4 broke the mass and dropped from 50% to 9%

[endgame] Do not let your lone bishop be the only defender of pawns: a rook attacking the bishop forces trade or loss of the whole queenside Example: 33.Rd6/34.Rc6 hit the b6 bishop until Bd6 Rxd6 won it and every pawn after

[endgame] Before your king captures material on the edge, count the pawn race: check your king stays inside the square of all enemy passers Example: 44...Kxh4 won a rook but f4-f5-f6 and h4-h8 promoted two queens unstoppably

[middlegame] Never trade queen for rook (or piece for two pawns) voluntarily; keep the queen to escort passers and give checks against a bare king Example: 26...Qc3 27.bxc3 turned a crushing attack into a hopeless bishop-versus-rook grind

[middlegame] Deny enemy knights and rooks the d3/c2/f3/6th-rank entry squares with a pawn or piece before they arrive, not after Example: Opponent's rook reached d6/c6 freely once my pawns no longer covered those squares

[endgame] With extra pawns, advance them with king support only; an unsupported push that frees a square for the enemy rook loses tempo and the pawn Example: 31...c5 vacated squares and let 32.Rd6 attack bishop and pawns at once
[opening] Before an exchange sequence on an open file, recount defenders of your central pawn after the trades Example: 8.a4 axb5 axb5 Rxa8 removed e4's guard and lost the pawn to ...Nxe4

[middlegame] Keep a bishop or knight on an advanced square only if a pawn supports it; otherwise it is a target that loses tempo Example: Bd5 and Be4 were chased by pawns because c4/d3 support never came

[middlegame] With a clear material edge, play the simplest consolidating developing move and trade pieces, not pawns; avoid clever maneuvers Example: Being a piece up, Be4 instead of Nc3 threw away most of the advantage in two moves

[endgame] Before simplifying, name the exact ending you are entering and confirm it is a known win; bishop+2 pawns versus rook is usually only a draw Example: Trading into rook-versus-bishop after Qc3 was objectively lost despite "extra pawns"
